By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.sgvtribune.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 23, 2026 at 10:17 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Is the answer to California’s housing crisis more bonds and more debt? Of course not.
Yet that’s what’s being pitched with Proposition 1.
Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature via Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), Prop. 1 asks voters to approve (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) $11.25 billion in bonds to help finance various programs, including a $500 million down payment assistance program.
One bond – $1.25 billion – will go toward the Department of Veteran Affairs (CalVet) Home Loan Program. Participants in the program will repay this portion of Prop. 1.
The other $10 billion bond will be paid out of the state’s General Fund, and will go toward various programs. Most of it will go toward subsidized housing for low-income residents, while other funds will go toward programs aimed at student housing, tribes and farmworkers.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, Prop. 1 “would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students.”
Proponents say Prop. 1 is worth the cost given the state’s high rate of homelessness and the high proportion of renters who struggle with high housing costs. In backing the measure, California YIMBY argues that, “Publicly-funded housing subsidies for low-income Californians who cannot afford market-rate rents are a good thing, and they should be more widely available.”
Yeah, no.
Taxpayer-subsidized housing in California is incredibly expensive to build. As a RAND Corp. report (https://backtobasicssj.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/RAND_RRA3743-1.pdf) from last year points out, publicly-subsidized “affordable” housing in California costs 1.5 times that of market rate housing “and more than four times the cost of market-rate housing in Texas.”
There are myriad reasons for this, of course. As much progress as California has made in loosening zoning laws, the state’s land-use policies remain restrictive. Permitting processes in major cities are often incredibly slow (https://x.com/esoltas/status/2098162675989565925/photo/1) . Reprieves from the California Environmental Quality Act always come with costly strings attached, including labor mandates.
Throwing more money into housing that’s slow and expensive to build simply won’t accomplish very much, because it can’t.
California YIMBY, to its credit, also points out some of the less desirable features of the measure. The down payment assistance program, for example, might be nice for those who benefit from it, but given the low supply of housing, it could end up contributing to higher home prices.
Then there’s the total bill for all of this. The $10 billion general obligation bond will, after interest, cost far more than that and further crowd-out other spending in the state budget. According to the LAO, the state will be spending $500 million to $600 million a year for 25 years to pay off the bond.
This, in turn, will only put further pressure on the perpetually precarious state budget and increase the risk of the Legislature approving or seeking new and higher taxes. This is no idle threat considering state lawmakers contemplated hundreds of billions of dollars (https://www.caltax.org/foundation/reports/20260611_Tax_and_Fee_Report.pdf) in new taxes this legislative session.
Eight years ago, in opposing the very similar Proposition 1 in 2018, we wrote (https://www.sgvtribune.com/2018/09/18/proposition-1-is-not-the-answer-to-our-housing-crisis-vote-no/) , “If California’s leaders are serious about making California a more affordable place to live, they should concentrate their efforts on curtailing onerous regulations and restrictive land-use policies and making it easier for homebuilders to build. And if they insist on subsidizing housing, they should do so directly, rather than wasting taxpayer money on interest payments.”
We stand by that, though we’d emphasize the need for California to stop fiddling and burdening reforms with mandates. There are those who argue California can both subsidize housing and loosen regulations, but the reality that we’re still having this discussion underscores that state and local leaders are dragging their feet and not deregulating fast enough.
California needs more housing, yes, but it doesn’t need Prop. 1.
Prop. 1 squanders billions into expensive housing and other gimmicks to buy political support.
Vote no and demand better housing policies.

I recently led a study that compared total apartment development costs in California to those in Colorado and Texas.

Land costs in California are over three times the Texas average.
“Hard costs,” or those related to improving the land and constructing buildings, are 2.2 times those in Texas.
California's “soft costs,” which include financing, architectural and engineering fees, and development fees charged by local governments, are 3.8 times the Texas average.
There are some unavoidable California-specific costs, like ensuring buildings are resilient to shaking from earthquakes.

Borrow $11.25 billion for housing
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

October 1, 2026
Dear friends,
I am pleased to submit the 2026 Debt Affordability Report to you, my last one as your State Treasurer and a document required to be sent annu-
ally to provide critical information regarding our general fund-supported bond programs. I am pleased to report that credit rating agencies and
investors alike continue to positively recognize California’s commitments to fiscal responsibility and transparency, demonstrated by our strong and
stable bond ratings and robust demand for our bonds. This recognition is critical to our ability to efficiently raise significant capital to build and
improve critical infrastructure throughout the state, including for housing, schools, roads, and many other projects that benefit our constituents.
My office’s continued commitment to meeting our debt obligations in full and on time has never been stronger and continues to endure across
market and economic cycles, maintaining our state’s market leadership as the benchmark issuer for the broader municipal bond market.
In the past fiscal year, my office expertly executed our state’s debt offerings despite continuing and enhanced volatility driven largely by federal
actions nationally and globally. During a year when inflation continued at over 3 percent, broad tariffs were legally invalidated and then partially re-
imposed, a federal government shutdown eliminated economic data releases for a significant period of time, our country went to war in Iran and a
new Federal Reserve chairman was seated, financial markets were volatile. Despite these major developments, however, artificial intelligence-related
themes continued to support the equity market while the bond market remained relatively stable through much of the fiscal year. However, in
March 2026 interest rates started to trend higher and as I deliver this report to you rates continue to climb, with the 10-year Treasury yield hitting a
20-year high in September. With higher interest rates comes a higher cost to service our debt, which can create other budget impacts and funding
tradeoffs. As a result, continued careful consideration of all legislation and policies that impact our fiscal health will be critical in the years ahead.
California’s overall debt profile remains stable. Our general obligation (GO) bond’s double-A credit ratings were reaffirmed by all three major
rating agencies in 2025-26. The rating agencies continue to cite the State’s large and diverse economic base, healthy liquidity and reserves,
and a stable long-term liability profile as key strengths, while noting ongoing structural challenges such as revenue volatility and exposure to
physical risks such as natural disasters. Our debt portfolio is largely and conservatively comprised of fixed rate debt, with variable rate exposure
maintained well below statutory and policy limits. Affordability indicators—such as debt service relative to general fund revenues and other
measures of leverage—remain within historical norms and continue to reflect the scale and diversity of the State’s economy. However, these
debt load measurements are also higher than many of the most populous states, so issuing debt at levels that significantly outpace economic
and budget growth is likely to erode our current strengths.
During the last fiscal year my office executed the issuance of $7.2 billion of general obligation bonds and $1.4 billion of lease revenue bonds,
all primarily secured by the general fund. Of these amounts, we sold $3.1 billion of refunding bonds that will produce $401 million of debt
service savings to the general fund over the life of the bonds. During my almost 8 years in office, I am proud that we refinanced debt that will
save the state’s general fund over $8.4 billion.
Looking ahead, my office anticipates continued issuance of general fund-supported bonds for both new money and refinancing purposes.
As of June 30, 2026, we have over $44 billion of authorized but unissued bonds, and voters will be asked in November to consider almost
$20 billion of additional general obligation bond authorization. As always, we will execute the sale of such bonds based on prudent financial
management principles in the interest of achieving the lowest cost to finance critical statewide capital investments.
My office stands ready to assist as you consider the State’s existing obligations and future financing needs. Thank you for your continued col-
laboration to manage our state’s debt in a fiscally responsible manner.
In Peace and Friendship,

PREFACE
Government Code Section 12330 requires the State Trea-
surer to submit an annual Debt Affordability Report (DAR)
to the Governor and Legislature. The report must provide
the following information:
• A listing of authorized but unissued debt supported by
the General Fund that the Treasurer intends to sell dur-
ing the current year (2026-27) and the following year
(2027-28), and the projected increase in debt service as
a result of those sales.
• A description of the market for state bonds.
• An analysis of state bonds’ credit ratings.
• A listing of outstanding debt supported by the General
Fund and a schedule of debt service requirements for
the debt.
• A listing of authorized but unissued bonds that would
be supported by the General Fund.
• Identification of pertinent debt ratios, such as debt service
to General Fund revenues, debt to personal income, debt
to estimated full value of property and debt per capita.
• A comparison of the pertinent debt ratios for the state
with those of the 10 most populous states.
• The percentage of the state’s outstanding general ob-
ligation (GO) bonds constituting fixed rate bonds,
variable rate bonds, bonds that have an effective fixed
interest rate through a hedging contract and bonds
that have an effective variable interest rate through a
hedging contract.
• A description of any hedging contract, the outstanding
face value, the effective date, the expiration date, the
name and ratings of the counterparty, the rate or float-
ing index paid by the state and the counterparty, and an
assessment of how the contract met its objectives.
NOTES ON TERMINOLOGY
• This report frequently uses the words “bonds” and “debt”
interchangeably, even when the underlying obligation se-
curing the bonds does not constitute debt subject to limi-
tation under California’s constitution. This conforms to
the municipal market convention that applies the terms
“debt” and “debt service” to a wide variety of fixed in-
come instruments, regardless of their precise legal status.
• The report references fiscal years without using the term
“fiscal year” or “fiscal.” For example, 2026-27 means the
2026-27 fiscal year ending June 30, 2027.

STATE TREASURER’S OFFICE1
California is one of the largest issuers in the $4 trillion U.S.
municipal bond market. Over the last five fiscal years, the
state has issued an average of $7.5 billion of General Obliga-
tion (GO) bonds annually. In 2025-26, the state issued $7.2
billion of GO bonds that were primarily payable from the
general fund. Of that total, $3.3 billion was sold to provide
funding for various voter approved GO bond acts, $784 mil-
lion was sold to retire GO commercial paper, $3.1 billion
was sold to refinance outstanding fixed rate GO bonds to
produce debt service savings, and $55 million was sold to
convert outstanding variable rate GO bonds into fixed rate
GO bonds.
Beyond the issuance of GO bonds and other general fund-
supported debt (the description of which is the subject of
this Debt Affordability Report (DAR) and further described
in subsequent sections), it is important to note that the state
and state-related entities (e.g., Department of Water Re-
sources, California State University System, UC Regents and
others) together issue “billions of dollars” of other types of
debt not supported by the state’s general fund. As a result,
while the state’s GO bond program is one of the single largest
debt programs in the nation, the bonds issued by the broader
universe of California issuers comprise a significant portion
of the overall U.S. municipal bond market every year. This
section focuses on the market for the state’s GO bonds; how-
ever, all state and state-related bond issuers are similarly im-
pacted by the overall bond market described in this section.
The market and price for the state’s GO bonds are influenced
by many factors specific to the state as well as overall condi-
tions in the financial markets. These factors include but are
not limited to the economy, general market interest rates,
significant domestic and global events, national and state
personal income tax rates, the supply of and demand for mu-
nicipal bonds, and investor perception of the state’s credit.
For the 12-month period from July 2025 to June 2026, the
municipal bond market has been influenced, by among other
things, Federal Reserve interest rate cuts, inflation driven in
part by tariffs and higher oil prices, various other economic
indicators, Federal government shutdowns, and important
geopolitical events. These influences on the market have re-
sulted in an uncertain interest rate environment. Overall, in-
terest rates have risen across the yield curve, which has main-
tained a generally upward sloping shape (i.e., higher yields are
generally associated with longer terms per security).
STATE-SPECIFIC FACTORS
One significant state-specific factor in determining the
interest cost of the state’s GO bonds is the credit ratings
assigned by the rating agencies to these bonds. Rating agen-
cies assign credit ratings based on many factors related to
issuers. For the state’s GO bonds, they consider state gov-
ernment revenues, expenditures, reserves, and long-term li-
abilities, as well as the underlying economy of the state. In
addition to the credit ratings, the rating agencies also assign
outlooks to their ratings based on trends that they believe
could lead to rating changes. Investors also consider similar
credit factors in determining their level of participation in
purchasing and holding the state’s GO bonds, which can
affect interest cost on the state’s GO bonds.
How the state handles changes in revenues, which have his-
torically been volatile because the state’s tax revenue system
relies heavily on high-income taxpayers, can impact how the
rating agencies or investors evaluate the state’s credit. When
revenues declined sharply, the state had to implement solu-
tions such as expenditure reductions, delays, fund shifts, and
the use of budget reserves to achieve balanced budgets. For
example, in 2022-23, after a period of unprecedented general
MARKET FOR STATE BONDSSECTION 1
2026 DEBT AFFORDABILITY REPORT2
fund revenue growth, the state faced a severe downturn in
revenues due to a then-declining stock market, high infla-
tion, and rising interest rates. The state declared fiscal emer-
gencies to achieve balanced budgets in its 2024 and 2025
Budget Acts, using a combination of expenditure reductions
and reserve withdrawals. Although revenues and transfers are
forecast to be higher starting in 2027-28, general fund short-
falls were still projected for 2026-27 and 2027-28 absent
further corrective measures. The 2026 Budget Act balanced
the budget using a combination of new revenue solutions,
expenditure reductions, and reserves to help close the short-
falls, while continuing to support critical investments in edu-
cation, mitigating the impacts of climate change, addressing
housing needs, and other important state priorities. Each of
these different types of budget solutions can be viewed differ-
ently from a credit perspective.
Additionally, it is important to note that the 2026 Budget
Act is based on a variety of estimates and assumptions, and
as a result, it faces numerous budgetary and economic risks
with potentially significant general fund impacts. These risks
include, among other things, volatility in the state’s revenues,
threat of an economic recession, significant reductions in fed-
eral funding or other federal actions that could impact the
state’s general fund, adverse decisions in lawsuits against the
state or its related entities, and the cost and persistent un-
funded liabilities related to public employee retirement bene-
fits. These risks are also among the factors that rating agencies
and investors consider in their analysis of the state’s credit.
In 2025-26, the ratings on the state’s GO bonds have re-
mained steady at “AA” by Fitch Ratings (Fitch), “Aa2” by
Moody’s Ratings (Moody’s) and “AA-” by S&P Global Rat-
ings (S&P). In addition, the state’s outlook from each credit
rating agency was “stable” throughout 2025-26.

INTEREST RATE TRENDS
In 2025-26, interest rates were comparatively stable versus
prior years by most measures. The relative stability reflected
shifting outlooks about the direction of inflation and the
economy over much of the year. Market participants reacted
to economic data to try to decipher the direction of future
policy actions by the Federal Reserve and other central banks.
When the data reflected higher inflation or a strengthening
economy, interest rates would rise, while lower inflation or
a weakening job market would lead to interest rate declines.
However, the insight from one set of data was often offset by
the next set of data, limiting the extent to which interest rates
changed. Nonetheless, there were several notable phases for
interest rate fluctuations as market sentiments changed.
For the first two months of 2025-26, the Federal Reserve was
maintaining a neutral interest rate policy stance after making
three rate cuts totaling 1 percent in 2024. It was watching the
economy for signs of a slowdown or inflation driven in part
by tariffs, and interest rates held largely steady. As a result,
interest rates generally moved in a narrow band.
Starting in September 2025, a lower court decision strik-
ing down tariffs enacted under the International Emergency
Economic Powers Act, lower inflation numbers, and weaker
economic data all helped to prompt the Federal Reserve to
cut rates by 25 bps in each of three consecutive meetings.
These developments brought about a decline in interest rates.
Interest rates continued to modestly decline as the Federal
government shut down in October 2025 due to a budgetary
impasse. Concerns over the effect of the Federal government
shutdown and the resulting absence of official economic data
continued to keep interest rates relatively low.
When the Federal government reopened, focus turned to
the number of potential rate cuts for 2026; when most
major market strategists priced in only one Federal Reserve
cut, interest rates rose modestly through January.
Then, the nomination of Federal Reserve chairman Warsh,
lower than expected CPI, and the Supreme Court ruling
on tariffs all helped lead to a decline in interest rates in
February 2026.
The U.S. attack of Iran in late February and the resulting
increase in oil prices renewed concerns over inflation and
pushed interest rates higher. Subsequently, news about the
conflict led oil prices and interest rates to fluctuate in the
last months of 2025-26. While outside of 2025-26, in Sep-
tember 2026 the Federal Reserve increased rates by 25 bps
citing the policy action will support a timelier return to the
committee’s 2 percent goal for inflation.

RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN TAX-EXEMPT
AND TAXABLE INTEREST RATES
As noted in the prior discussion, many of the factors that
influence U.S. Treasury rates also impact municipal bond
interest rates. As a result, there exists an observably strong
correlation between U.S. Treasury yields and tax-exempt
municipal bond rates. Figure 6 depicts the changes in
taxable 10-year U.S. Treasury yields and the national tax-
exempt 10-year AAA GO MMD benchmark index from
July 2025 through June 2026. As the data shows, the two
measures generally move with a similar pattern, evidencing
the strong correlation between the two markets.
While their movements are correlated, the precise relation-
ship between them can shift over time, as they can react
somewhat differently to underlying influences. Municipal
bond market participants monitor this relationship, mea-
suring it as the ratio between the AAA GO MMD bench-
mark index and the corresponding U.S. Treasury yield.

INTEREST RATES ON THE STATE’S GO BONDS
Interest rates on the state’s GO bonds are the product of
both state-specific factors and general market conditions.
Over the course of 2025-26, interest rates on the state’s GO
bonds have largely followed the same trend as the national
AAA GO MMD benchmark. However, the declining credit
spreads of the state’s GO bonds mean that the overall in-
crease has not been quite as significant as that of the national
AAA GO MMD benchmark. Figure 8 compares California
GO MMD benchmark rates from the end of 2024-25 to
the end of 2025-26. Overall, the 2025-26 interest rates for
the state’s GO Bonds are lower than those seen in 2024-25,
although they remain elevated as compared to rates from
much of the past decade as shown in Figure 9.
Although interest rates have been comparatively high this
past fiscal year, the state was still able to refinance $3.3 bil-
lion of its outstanding GO bonds in 2025-26 to reduce debt
service costs. These refinancings generated approximately
$401 million of total debt service savings over the remain-
ing life of the bonds that were refinanced, or approximately
$314 million on a present value basis.
In addition to fixed-rate GO bonds, the state has issued
variable rate GO bonds to reduce interest cost and to help
diversify its capital structure. As of June 30, 2026, the
state had a total of approximately $1.2 billion in outstand-
ing variable rate GO debt. The state’s variable interest
rates have continued to be a source of low-cost financing
throughout the year. Historically, short-term tax-exempt
interest rates, such as those on variable rate GO bonds,
have been lower than long-term tax-exempt interest rates.
Figure 10 shows the performance of the state’s variable rate
GO bonds in 2025-26 in comparison to the short-term
Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association
(SIFMA) swap index, which is a composite national index
of tax-exempt seven-day high-grade variable rate demand
obligations similar to the state’s variable rate GO bonds.
As shown, the state’s variable rate GO bonds performed
very favorably against the national SIFMA index, averag-
ing approximately one percent lower than the index.

OVERVIEW
Figure 11 summarizes the state’s long-term debt as of June
30, 2026. This summary of state debt includes general fund-
supported GO bonds approved by voters and lease revenue
bonds (LRBs) authorized by the Legislature, as well as self-
liquidating GO bonds. LRBs are secured by lease payments
payable from the operating budgets of the respective lessees
which are primarily but not exclusively derived from the gen-
eral fund. Self-liquidating GO bonds receive revenues from
specified sources so that money from the general fund is not
expected to pay debt service. However, the general fund is
obligated to pay debt service should the designated revenues
to support repayment not be sufficient. The figures include
bonds the state has sold and not yet repaid (outstanding) and
bonds authorized but not yet sold. A detailed list of the state’s
outstanding bonds, and their debt service requirements, can
be found in Appendices A and B, respectively.
• As of June 30, 2026, approximately 98.4 percent of the
state’s outstanding GO bonds had fixed interest rates
and 1.6 percent of the state’s outstanding GO bonds
had variable interest rates. The amount of outstanding
variable rate GO bonds is lower than the statutorily au-
thorized maximum of 20 percent. The State Treasurer
has adopted a Debt Management Policy that, as of the
date hereof, further reduces this limitation on variable
rate indebtedness to 10 percent of the aggregate amount
of long-term GO bonds outstanding.
• The state has no interest rate hedging contracts on any
debt discussed in this report.
INTENDED ISSUANCE OF GENERAL
FUND-SUPPORTED BONDS
The State Treasurer’s Office (STO) estimates of intended is-
suance are based on Department of Finance (DOF) projec-
tions of state departments’ funding needs. Projections for
new-money debt issuance are based on a variety of factors
and are periodically updated. Factors that could affect the
amount of issuance include actual spending by depart-
ments, revised funding needs, overall budget constraints,
use or repayment of commercial paper, general market con-
ditions and other considerations. Actual issuance amounts
often vary significantly from initial estimates.
Figure 12 shows the STO’s initial estimated issuance of
new-money general fund-supported bonds over the current
and next fiscal year as of August 1, 2026. Only currently
authorized but unissued GO bonds are reflected in Figure
12. The estimated issuance may increase should new bond
measures be approved. Two GO bond measures will be on
the November 3, 2026, state ballot. If both are approved, an
additional $19.65 billion would be added to the authorized
but unissued GO bonds amount, of which $1.25 billion
would be self liquidating GO bonds as shown in Figure 11.
As shown in Figure 12, the STO preliminarily estimates the
state will issue a combined $16.9 billion of new money gen-
eral fund-supported bonds in 2026-27 and 2027-28. Us-
ing these assumptions for debt issuance, the STO estimates
debt service payments from the general fund will increase
by $82.8 million in 2026-27 and $795.7 million in 2027-
28.3 A detailed list of the estimated debt service require-
ments can be found in Appendix B.

DEBT AS PERCENTAGE OF PERSONAL INCOME
Comparing a state’s level of debt to the total personal in-
come of its residents is a way to measure a state’s ability to
generate revenues and repay its obligations. In Moody’s Sec-
tor Profile - U.S. States report dated September 24, 2026
titled “Medians - Higher Rates and Robust Returns Reduce
Pension Liabilities Further” (“Moody’s September 2026 Re-
port”), Moody’s lists the state’s ratio of net tax-supported
debt8 to personal income at 2.8 percent.
DEBT PER CAPITA
Debt per capita measures residents’ average share of a state’s
total outstanding debt. It does not account for the employ-
ment status, income, or other financial resources of resi-
dents. As a result, debt per capita does not reflect a state’s
ability to repay its obligations as well as other ratios, such
as debt service as a percentage of General Fund revenues or
debt as a percentage of personal income. In Moody’s Sep-
tember 2026 Report, Moody’s lists the state’s net tax sup-
ported debt8 per capita at $2,561.
MEASURING DEBT BURDENSECTION 3
DEBT RATIOS
Measuring California’s debt level with various ratios provides
one way to compare the state’s debt burden to that of other
borrowers even if it does not directly define or address debt
affordability. The three most used ratios are net tax supported
debt service as a percentage of General Fund revenues, debt
as a percentage of personal income, and debt per capita. A
fourth ratio – debt as a percentage of state gross domestic
product (GDP) – can also be a useful comparison tool.
DEBT SERVICE AS PERCENTAGE OF
GENERAL FUND REVENUES
Because debt service is considered a fixed part of a budget,
credit analysts compare general fund-supported debt service
to general fund revenues to measure a state’s fiscal flexibility.
California’s ratio of general fund-supported debt service to
general fund revenues was 3.41 percent4 in 2025-26. That
figure is based on $8.14 billion5 of GO and LRB debt ser-
vice payments versus $238.7 billion of general fund revenues
(less transfers from the Budget Stabilization Account/Rainy
Day Fund (BSA))6. The STO estimates this ratio will be 3.83
percent7 in 2026-27. That estimate is based on an expected
$8.68 billion of debt service payments versus $226.8 billion

notes, tobacco securitization bonds with a general fund backstop, No Place Like Home bonds, and other governmental debts as determined by Moody’s.

DEBT AS PERCENTAGE OF STATE GDP
Debt as a percentage of GDP is generally used to measure
the financial leverage provided by an issuer’s economy. Spe-
cifically, this debt ratio compares what an issuer owes ver-
sus what it produces. California has one of the largest and
most diverse economies in the world. In Moody’s Septem-
ber 2026 Report, Moody’s lists the state’s net tax-supported
debt8 as a percentage of state GDP at 2.4 percent.
DEBT RATIOS OF THE 10 MOST POPULOUS STATES
It is useful to compare California’s debt levels with those of
its “peer group” of the 10 most populous states. As shown in
the tables, the median for the 10 most populous states’ debt
to personal income (Figure 13), debt per capita (Figure 14)
and debt as a percentage of GDP (Figure 15) are, on aver-
age, lower than California’s calculated ratios.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 11, 2026 at 5:40 PM PDT

From 2000 to 2024, according to Ballotpedia (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_2,_Use_Millionaire%27s_Tax_Revenue_for_Homelessness_Prevention_Housing_Bonds_Measure_(2018)), California voters approved eight housing measures. Most of their $17 billion-plus in funding came from state bonds. Some measures focused on adding “affordable housing” in general; some on helping veterans; some on sheltering the homeless. All were billed as obvious, straightforward responses to a chronic housing shortage.
But none laid a glove on the problem. When “affordable” units cost $800,000 or more to build, billions in funding doesn’t add enough housing to matter in a state with 39 million people.
The extreme cost of housing remains the main reason a state whose leaders love to boast about how big its economy is has the highest percentage of impoverished residents (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/09/california-living-costs-highest-poverty/) in the nation. The epicenter of American poverty isn’t a grim, jobs-starved metro area in the Deep South or Appalachia, it’s Los Angeles County (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/09/california-living-costs-highest-poverty/).
So why do state politicians keep asking voters to approve costly, ineffective initiatives? Because the “Message: I care” optics of such measures allow these pols to insist they actually care about California’s extreme cost of living.
Which brings us to Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)), placed on the November ballot by the Legislature. It would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build “affordable” housing that is only affordable to the relative handful of residents lucky enough to get a taxpayer-subsidized unit. With broad institutional support, little opposition and a smart campaign that focuses on how the measure prioritizes helping veterans, it seems sure to pass.
But the U-T Editorial Board opposes costly propositions — whose bonds must be paid off for decades to come — if their primary effect is to create an illusion of progress. As progressive reformers Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson pointed out (https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/book-review-abundance) in “Abundance,” their persuasive 2025 book, many influential California Democrats value process over results. They see signaling their shared values to party voters as more important than their performance in office.
This is particularly unfortunate because if voters this November approve Proposition 45 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/11/endorsement-yes-on-prop-45-to-reform-ceqa-limit-state-dysfunction/) — reducing the tools in CEQA that have been used for 50-plus years to block housing construction — state lawmakers would have a real opportunity to create change. According to Princeton economist Evan Soltas’ review (https://x.com/esoltas/status/2098162675989565925/photo/1) of 60 large U.S. cities, it takes longer or nearly as long to get a single-family home building permit in San Francisco, Los Angeles or San Diego as it does to permit and build such a home in Indianapolis, Fort Worth or Colorado Springs. The time it takes to get a permit and to build a home directly correlates with its final cost.
To fix the housing mess, CEQA reforms should only be the start.
Reducing the state’s hostility to non-union construction companies would help.
So would new thinking about zoning that frees up hundreds of square miles of agricultural parcels for housing.
So would embracing the sturdy new versions of inexpensive prefabricated homes that have been very popular in Japan (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/) and Great Britain (https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/apr/14/fast-build-modular-homes-an-answer-to-the-uk-housing-crisis).
So would passage of a bill that would fix flawed regulations that have the effect of incentivizing lawsuits against condo builders; such a measure (Assembly Bill 1903) died in the Capitol two weeks ago without ever drawing a single “no” vote (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/) in the Assembly or Senate.
This specific and constructive agenda could make a real difference. But for a dozen years, lawmakers have preferred posturing about the housing status quo to meaningfully addressing it.
Proposition 1 is one more example.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 23, 2026 at 10:17 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Is the answer to California’s housing crisis more bonds and more debt? Of course not.
Yet that’s what’s being pitched with Proposition 1.
Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature via Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), Prop. 1 asks voters to approve (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) $11.25 billion in bonds to help finance various programs, including a $500 million down payment assistance program.
One bond – $1.25 billion – will go toward the Department of Veteran Affairs (CalVet) Home Loan Program. Participants in the program will repay this portion of Prop. 1.
The other $10 billion bond will be paid out of the state’s General Fund, and will go toward various programs. Most of it will go toward subsidized housing for low-income residents, while other funds will go toward programs aimed at student housing, tribes and farmworkers.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, Prop. 1 “would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students.”
Proponents say Prop. 1 is worth the cost given the state’s high rate of homelessness and the high proportion of renters who struggle with high housing costs. In backing the measure, California YIMBY argues that, “Publicly-funded housing subsidies for low-income Californians who cannot afford market-rate rents are a good thing, and they should be more widely available.”
Yeah, no.
Taxpayer-subsidized housing in California is incredibly expensive to build. As a RAND Corp. report (https://backtobasicssj.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/RAND_RRA3743-1.pdf) from last year points out, publicly-subsidized “affordable” housing in California costs 1.5 times that of market rate housing “and more than four times the cost of market-rate housing in Texas.”
There are myriad reasons for this, of course. As much progress as California has made in loosening zoning laws, the state’s land-use policies remain restrictive. Permitting processes in major cities are often incredibly slow (https://x.com/esoltas/status/2098162675989565925/photo/1) . Reprieves from the California Environmental Quality Act always come with costly strings attached, including labor mandates.
Throwing more money into housing that’s slow and expensive to build simply won’t accomplish very much, because it can’t.
California YIMBY, to its credit, also points out some of the less desirable features of the measure. The down payment assistance program, for example, might be nice for those who benefit from it, but given the low supply of housing, it could end up contributing to higher home prices.
Then there’s the total bill for all of this. The $10 billion general obligation bond will, after interest, cost far more than that and further crowd-out other spending in the state budget. According to the LAO, the state will be spending $500 million to $600 million a year for 25 years to pay off the bond.
This, in turn, will only put further pressure on the perpetually precarious state budget and increase the risk of the Legislature approving or seeking new and higher taxes. This is no idle threat considering state lawmakers contemplated hundreds of billions of dollars (https://www.caltax.org/foundation/reports/20260611_Tax_and_Fee_Report.pdf) in new taxes this legislative session.
Eight years ago, in opposing the very similar Proposition 1 in 2018, we wrote (https://www.ocregister.com/2018/09/18/proposition-1-is-not-the-answer-to-our-housing-crisis-vote-no/) , “If California’s leaders are serious about making California a more affordable place to live, they should concentrate their efforts on curtailing onerous regulations and restrictive land-use policies and making it easier for homebuilders to build. And if they insist on subsidizing housing, they should do so directly, rather than wasting taxpayer money on interest payments.”
We stand by that, though we’d emphasize the need for California to stop fiddling and burdening reforms with mandates. There are those who argue California can both subsidize housing and loosen regulations, but the reality that we’re still having this discussion underscores that state and local leaders are dragging their feet and not deregulating fast enough.
California needs more housing, yes, but it doesn’t need Prop. 1.
Prop. 1 squanders billions into expensive housing and other gimmicks to buy political support.
Vote no and demand better housing policies.

Initial Comments on the Governor's May Revision
Introduction
May Revision Balanced on Higher Revenues and Reserves

Executive Summary
Despite Revenue Boom, Budget Architecture Relies on $20 Billion in Reserves. The May Revision's
estimate of tax revenues in the current year represents over 30 percent growth from three years ago.
Much of this growth is driven by the personal income tax, which is up nearly 50 percent during that
same period. Periods of elevated revenues like these are typically when the state should be strengthening
its fiscal position. Instead, the May Revision draws it down-relying on roughly $20 billion in reserve withdrawals
and suspended deposits, as well as $4 billion in borrowing (on top of tens of billions of dollars in
existing borrowing), to achieve budget balance.
Structural Problem Is Now Upon the State. For several years, we have cautioned that
structural deficits were emerging and would soon require corrective action. Despite the current revenue
boom, the state now faces a structural budget imbalance-meaning ongoing revenues are insufficient to support
ongoing expenditures.
Future Deficits Have Come Down Substantially, but State Ill‑Prepared for a Slip Up in
Revenues. In January, we noted that our office and the administration estimated the
state faced future deficits between $20 billion and $30 billion per year. Due to a combination of
higher revenue estimates, lower baseline spending, and ongoing proposals (which both raise revenue and
reduce spending), the May Revision cuts these future deficits in half. Despite this progress, the underlying
budget condition is not sound. First, the existence of any operating deficits during a revenue boom
of this magnitude is itself a warning sign. Further, given the state's diminished reserves and already
accumulated wall of debt, California is ill‑prepared for even a slip up in revenues. Even just a
repeat of the 2022 market declines, which were mild by historical standards, could quickly push the budget
into deep deficits. Alarmingly, given current market conditions, the dot‑com bust probably is a better
parallel. If such scenario were to repeat, the revenue hole could be $100 billion.
Recommendations. The state's current fiscal situation is genuinely
unprecedented. Despite booming revenues, the budget position is overextended, reflecting: a structurally
higher spending base, diminished reserves, an already accumulated wall of debt, and an
operating deficit. As such, we recommend the Legislature take action to put the budget on sound
fiscal footing, including:
Maintaining Amount of Ongoing Solutions Proposed by Governor. We recommend the
Legislature maintain at least the amount of ongoing solutions included in the May Revision.
Making a $20 Billion Discretionary Reserve Deposit. In light
of current revenue conditions, we recommend the Legislature make a $20 billion discretionary
deposit into the Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) this year. This would make notable progress toward
the administration's proposal that the state raise BSA reserves to 20 percent of General Fund
tax revenues.
Setting Aside $4 Billion for Potential Settle‑Up Obligation.
We recommend the Legislature set aside $4 billion to pre‑fund this likely
obligation.
Taken together, these recommendations require the state to identify roughly $24 billion in new budget capacity-or solutions-relative to the Governor's May Revision. The
Legislature could make significant progress toward this total by rejecting the proposals to set aside nearly
$10 billion for next year and about $1 billion in new discretionary spending.
Introduction
On May 14, 2026, Governor Newsom presented a revised state budget proposal to the Legislature. This annual
proposed revised budget is referred to as the May Revision. In this report, we provide a summary of and comments
on this revised budget, focusing on the overall condition of the state General Fund-the budget's main operating account. In the coming days,
we will analyze the plan in more detail and provide additional comments in hearing testimony.
(The information presented in this brief is based on our understanding of the administration's
proposals as of May 15, 2026. In many areas, our understanding of the proposals will continue to evolve.)
May Revision Balanced on Higher Revenues and Reserves
Higher Revenues Improve Budget Condition. Relative to the Governor's budget, the
administration's May Revision estimate of revenues across the budget window (2024‑25 to
2026‑27) are higher by about $16 billion. This upgrade is almost entirely attributable to
expectations for income tax collections, which are being driven by enthusiasm around artificial intelligence
(AI) and the related stock market boom. This improves the budget's bottom line.
Higher Spending Somewhat Offsets Higher Revenues. Under two initiatives, the State
Constitution requires the state to set aside a share of revenues for schools and community colleges
(Proposition 98, 1988) and debt payments and reserve deposits (Proposition 2, 2014). In line with the
administration's higher revenue estimates, both these requirements are also up. Across the rest of the
budget, however, spending is slightly lower, largely reflecting updated estimates of state employee pension
costs, which are driven by a technical correction.
Solutions and Discretionary Choices in May Revision
Solutions
The May Revision includes $14 billion in solutions in 2025‑26 and 2026‑27 as shown Figure 1. This includes: $2 billion in
revenue‑related proposals, nearly $3 billion in spending‑related solutions (including spending
reductions and fund shifts), $4 billion in new borrowing, and suspended reserve deposits of more than
$5 billion. These solutions reflect all of those included in the May Revision, as well as those originally
proposed in January. The remainder of this section walks through each of these components in more detail.
Revenue‑Related Solutions
Proposes Larger Managed Care Organization (MCO) Tax. The MCO tax is a specific tax on
health plans (such as Kaiser Permanente and Anthem Blue Cross) that helps pay for Medi‑Cal. It currently
provides around $7 billion to $8 billion annually. It is set to expire at the end of 2026. The
Governor's budget assumed renewal of the tax in 2027, but at a much lower level-just tens of millions of dollars in annual revenue. The
expected sizable reduction reflected the administration's understanding of recent federal and state policy
changes. The administration now believes it can pursue a larger tax and remain legally compliant. Accordingly,
the May Revision proposes a 2027 MCO tax that provides around $2 billion annually. The Governor proposes
using all of the revenue to offset General Fund costs in Medi‑Cal, resulting in annual savings of
$575 million in 2026‑27 and around $2 billion in subsequent years.
Proposes Permanent Limit on Business Tax Credits. California allows corporations to
claim a variety of tax credits that reduce their tax liability on a dollar‑for‑dollar basis.
Taxpayers that have enough credits are allowed to reduce their tax bill down to $800. Under the May Revision,
beginning in 2027, businesses would only be allowed to use tax credits to reduce their corporation tax liability
by 50 percent or $5 million, whichever is greater. In contrast to recent limits on business
credits, this change would be permanent. The administration estimates this would increase corporation tax
revenues by $850 million in 2026‑27 and $1.7 billion in 2027‑28.
Apply Sales Tax to Retail Sales of Digital Prewritten Software. Software not customized
for a particular client is called prewritten software. The state's sales tax currently applies to
prewritten software delivered on tangible media but not to other sales of software. The May Revision proposes to
apply the state's sales tax to prewritten software delivered in other ways-such as downloads and remote access-beginning in 2027. Custom software would remain exempt.
The administration estimates that this would raise General Fund revenue by $450 million and local
sales tax revenue by $560 million in 2026‑27, growing to $900 million General Fund and
$1.1 billion local revenue in 2027‑28.
Spending‑Related Solutions
Expands Package of Medi‑Cal Solutions. The May Revision includes additional
spending‑related budget solutions in Medi‑Cal relative to the Governor's budget. In
2026‑27, the additional savings would be $1.8 billion, mostly from a limited‑term proposal to
use more funding from Proposition 35 (2024) to help pay for Medi‑Cal provider rate increases.
The May Revision also includes several new ongoing solutions, including proposals to lower the asset limit
for seniors and persons with disabilities and to increase the monthly premium charged to adults with
unsatisfactory immigration status. Including proposals from January, the May Revision solutions associated with
Medi‑Cal are $2.2 billion in 2026‑27, including $400 million in reductions and
$1.8 billion in fund shifts.
All Other Spending‑Related Solutions Total $500 Million. Across the rest of the budget, the May Revision
includes $500 million in other spending‑related solutions (including both proposals that persist from
January and new proposals in May). These are relatively evenly split between spending reductions and fund
shifts. For example, other spending‑related solutions include: about $200 million in behavioral
health offsets across a variety of departments, $50 million in savings to align In‑Home Supportive
Services eligibility with Medi‑Cal, and $50 million in a reduction in the cost‑of‑living
adjustment for child care.
Borrowing
May Revision Includes $4 Billion "Settle‑Up" Obligation. The
May Revision generates a $4 billion settle‑up payment by providing less than the constitutionally
required funding level for schools and community colleges in 2025‑26. (The Governor's budget had
proposed a larger settle‑up payment of nearly $6 billion.) Settle up gives the state more budget
capacity this year, but if revenues meet expectations for 2025‑26 it would eventually require the state to
make a payment of this amount to schools and community college districts. (Conversely, if revenues fall short of
their projections, the state's settle‑up obligation would decline.) We understand this proposal is
intended, in part, to acknowledge revenue risks and avoid unintentionally spending more than the minimum
requirement if revenues decline and the requirement drops.
May Revision Would Bring Total Borrowing Close to $30 Billion. Recent budgets have relied on over
$25 billion in budgetary borrowing to close budget gaps. These are amounts that will need to be repaid in
the coming years-most of which will add to the state's
existing structural deficits. We call this budgetary borrowing the state's new "wall of
debt," in line with a Great Recession era term that described budgetary borrowing accumulated to partially
address the state's persistent budget problems. The May Revision proposal to create nearly $4 billion
in settle up would add to the wall of debt by that amount. (The May Revision also reflects some repayments of
certain debts.)
Suspended Reserve Deposits
Suspends Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) True‑Up Deposit of $5.4 Billion. Proposition 2 outlines
the formulas by which the state must, each year, make deposits into the BSA, unless those requirements are
suspended under a budget emergency. Proposition 2 also requires the state to revisit-or "true up"-its estimates of BSA deposits
twice: once in each subsequent fiscal year. These true‑ups are required even if the initial deposit was
suspended; however, true‑ups can themselves be suspended, as well. The state already suspended a
$1.6 billion initial deposit for 2025‑26. Under the administration's revenue estimates, an
additional $5.4 billion true‑up deposit is now required for that year. The May Revision proposes the
state suspend this entire true‑up deposit.
New Commitments
Revenue and Spending Commitments
New Discretionary Proposals of $1.3 Billion. The May Revision includes
$1.3 billion in new discretionary proposals (some of which were proposed at Governor's budget). These
use budget capacity and mean that more solutions are required to balance the budget. This entire amount is
driven almost exclusively by many small proposals rather than a few larger proposals. For example, some of the
largest of these items are: $76 million for utility replacement and site improvements at Exposition Park; a
$68 million reappropriation for broadband last‑mile infrastructure; and $56 million for a
disaster rebuilding program. The remainder of the list includes about 100 proposals, mostly less than
$20 million. (This also includes $25 million for one new revenue‑related proposal in
2026‑27 which grows to $100 million in 2027‑28.)
Discretionary Reserves and Set‑Asides
Sets Discretionary Reserve Balance to $4.5 Billion. The Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties
(SFEU) is a general‑purpose reserve commonly used to provide capacity for unanticipated expenditures,
including state costs associated with disasters and other emergencies. On a technical basis, it can be thought
of as the end balance of the state's General Fund-the money
that remains after accounting for all of the state's expected revenues and spending. The State
Constitution has a balanced budget requirement, which means the balance of the SFEU must be set above zero for
the upcoming fiscal year (2026‑27). Any level above that is up to the discretion of the Legislature. As a
result, we consider the entire balance of the SFEU to be a discretionary choice. That said, recent budgets have
set the SFEU between $3.5 billion and $4.5 billion, so the Governor's budget proposal to set the
balance to $4.5 billion is in line with recent policy.
Deposits $10 Billion
Into Temporary Surplus Holding Account (TSHA). The May Revision proposes a
first‑time deposit of nearly $10 billion into the TSHA-an account created to help the state avoid overcommitting a
surplus when revenues are surging. That said, although revenues are currently surging, by our count, there is no
"surplus" to overcommit. The box below describes this account and proposal in more detail.
What Is the Temporary Surplus Holding Account (TSHA)?
Revenues Are Both Volatile and Uncertain. State revenues are
volatile -they can grow or shrink rapidly from year to year, particularly because
California's tax system relies heavily high‑income taxpayers. This means that, in some years,
the state will collect significantly less in tax revenue than it has in spending commitments-resulting in large budget problems. Relatedly, there
is significant uncertainty about near‑term revenue estimates-that is, even for the upcoming fiscal year, revenues
can come in significantly above or below projections, resulting in large forecasting errors. This is
especially common when revenues are growing or shrinking rapidly. Reserves can help address both challenges-volatility and uncertainty. Historically, however,
the state's reserves have primarily been used to manage revenue volatility across economic cycles
rather than short‑term uncertainty in forecasting.
TSHA Was Set Up to Avoid Overspending a Surplus. In 2024, the Legislature created
the TSHA as a tool intended to manage near‑term revenue uncertainty. As we understand it, the account
was designed for periods when the state is experiencing surpluses during rapid revenue growth and might
otherwise risk committing to new spending based on uncertain revenue estimates that might not materialize.
The Legislature initially considered establishing formulas or rules governing deposits into the account.
Ultimately, however, the TSHA was enacted as a flexible and largely discretionary mechanism.
Governor Proposes Using TSHA for First Time in May Revision. The May Revision
proposes depositing $9.7 billion into the TSHA in 2026‑27 and withdrawing the same amount in
2027‑28. We understand the administration derived this amount from the remaining resources available
after accounting for baseline costs, budget solutions, and new proposals, including a Special Fund for
Economic Uncertainties balance of $4.5 billion. In effect, the TSHA proposal uses anticipated resources
from 2026‑27 to help balance the budget in 2027‑28.
Budget Condition
Budget Condition This Year
Figure 2 shows the General Fund condition under the May Revision. The
state would end 2026‑27 with $4.5 billion in the SFEU. The SFEU is the state's operating
reserve and essentially functions like an end‑of‑year balance. The State Constitution prohibits the
state from enacting a negative SFEU for the upcoming fiscal year, in this case 2026‑27.

content.thinking:
I've got the fiscal picture now: the LAO sees a structural budget imbalance, with its estimate of future deficits roughly halved, and it warns that the state is poorly placed to absorb even a modest revenue slip. I'm also weighing its dot-com scenario, where the revenue hole could reach about $100 billion.

I'm now pulling the Treasurer's October report: the debt service ratio is up to about 3.8%, and the report warns that issuing debt faster than the economy and budget grow could wear down the state's strengths. I'm also noting the roughly $44 billion in authorized but unissued bonds, plus the extra $19.65 billion that Props 1 and 38 would add if both pass.

Now I'm checking how the opposition frames Prop 1: the Union-Tribune calls it another round of failed state housing policy, and the OC Register argues more debt won't fix the problem. I'm also noting that Prop 45 could come up as a possible complement to it.

Next I'm looking at whether the Homekey and state audit critiques need to go in for balance, and I'm planning to search for recent state auditor findings on those programs. I also want to verify the CalMatters report on roughly 40,000 approved affordable units stalled by funding gaps, and check how the 2018 housing bond was committed and how many units it produced.

I'm now comparing the 2018 Prop 1 output with this proposal: the 2018 bond's roughly $3 billion produced about 22,735 units, which works out to around $132,000 per unit in state subsidy. Prop 1 is larger, with about $10 billion aimed at up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, so I'm checking whether the per-unit cost holds up at that scale.

I'm comparing the LAO's per-unit subsidy estimates for Prop 1 against the 2018 bond's results, since the numbers suggest the cost per unit could be quite different at this scale. I also want to check how the LAO's 2018 analysis projected unit counts, though that may not be necessary. There's a separate 2024 Prop 1 that could cause confusion, but I don't think it needs to be covered here.

I'm checking the KQED guide's "No" text, which may be a drafted argument rather than an official one, and I'm noting its framing: that the state should cut costly regulations before borrowing more. I'm also confirming how SPUR and the LAO each describe the scale of the roughly 40,000 rental units.

I'm going to check whether the KQED guide actually lists the opponents I'm expecting, like Carl DeMaio, Tony Strickland, or groups such as Howard Jarvis and the California Taxpayers Association. Next I'll pull the PRI post, the CalMatters March 2026 piece on the roughly 40,000 stalled units, and run a search for state auditor findings.

content.text: The fiscal picture is clearer now: the LAO describes a structural budget problem, and the Treasurer warns about debt growing faster than the budget. Next I'll check the opposition list in KQED's guide, the Pacific Research Institute's position, and the source for the "40,000 stalled units" claim.

Proposition 1
Should the state be authorized to issue $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to support building and preserving affordable housing, expanding homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income residents, veterans and homelessness programs?
The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 would authorize a general obligation bond, $10 billion of which would fund affordable housing and related infrastructure projects. Another $1.25 billion would fund the CalVet Home Loan Program. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) reports bond funds would support up to 40,000 rental units and could also assist 40,000 families in buying a home.
Yes Argument
Proposition 1 builds and preserves affordable homes and expands homeownership opportunities without raising taxes. It unlocks federal matching funds and fast-tracks construction. This measure will benefit veterans, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, at-risk foster youth, working families and people with disabilities.
No Argument
This package represents $11 billion in debt that taxpayers will add to their credit card with no reforms. We know the cost of building in California is exponentially higher than it needs to be. We have to reform that by first cutting costly regulations before we take out the credit card and borrow money.

Didn’t We Just Vote on Proposition 1? Ballot Numbers Add to Confusion

When reviewing your sample ballot and seeing Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/), the housing bond measure, you might ask yourself – didn’t we just vote on Proposition 1?
This November, Californians will decide the fate of 14 different statewide ballot measures. While it sounds exhausting, we’ve voted on more (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/BallotByType) in the past – a whopping 29 in the November 1988 election and 28 in the 1990 general election.
Adding to the confusion are the ballot proposition numbers themselves.
When reviewing your sample ballot and seeing Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/), the housing bond measure, you might ask yourself – didn’t we just vote on Proposition 1?
The answer is yes – Proposition 1 in the March 2024 primary dealt with mental health bond funding (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2024/primary/propositions/1/index.htm).
We also voted on Proposition 1 in November 2022 when voters decided on the so-called right to reproductive freedom (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2022/general/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) constitutional amendment.
Aren’t the numbers of the propositions supposed to grow over a certain number of years? So, why are we always voting on Proposition 1?
The answer lies with Sacrament politicians manipulating the system to try and maximize the chances of their favorite ballot measure passing.
Under California law (https://leginfo.ca.gov/pub/95-96/bill/asm/ab_3051-3100/ab_3092_bill_960606_chaptered.html), the numbers assigned to statewide ballot measures are supposed to run in a continuous sequence starting with 1 over a 10-year period, starting with the 1998 election. In 2028, we should flip back to voting on Prop. 1 once again. Before that, the numbers climbed sequentially election after election. There would be some duplication, but over a reasonable number of years so as not to confuse voters.
Then state lawmakers started getting involved by putting their thumb on the scale to boost the chances of their favorite ballot measures.
In 2022, Democratic lawmakers passed SB 131 (https://sfa.senate.ca.gov/sites/sfa.senate.ca.gov/files/packet/trp_7.3.24.pd) to move the abortion measure to the top of the ballot. In March 2024, lawmakers curiously voted to make the mental health bond Prop. 1 even thought it was the only measure on the ballot (this is another example of lawmaker tinkering; Democrats enacted Senate Bill 202 (https://www.leginfo.ca.gov/pub/11-12/bill/sen/sb_0201-0250/sb_202_bill_20110914_enrolled.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) in 2011 to only allow legislative ballot measures to be voted on during the June primary).
We had repeats of Propositions 2 through 6 in November 2024, which the rest of the initiatives numbered 32 through 36.
This year, we have a repeat of Propositions 1 through 5, with the rest of the measures numbered 37 through 45. Typically, the renumber of ballot measures by the Legislature only covers measures that lawmakers themselves vote to place on the ballot. Curiously, this year’s batch tries to boost the fortunes of a measure placed on the ballot by teachers’ unions and other special interest groups to make “permanent” a temporary tax for education funding, not through a vote of lawmakers.
Another interesting case was last year’s vote on Prop. 50. The reasoning behind picking the number out of thin air was campaign semantics – Gov. Newsom picked it (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2025/08/21/governor-newsom-signs-election-rigging-response-act-legislative-package-gives-people-power-to-push-back-on-trumps-attempts-to-shred-democracy/) to promote “fair elections in all 50 states.” Ironically, he did so by making California elections far less fair by bringing back the gerrymandering of congressional districts.
What’s the point of all of this? Does having Proposition 1 numbering help a ballot measure’s chance of passage? Research has shown not really.
USC economist and political scientist John Matsusaka has published the definitive work on the subject, reviewing the impact of ballot order in proposition elections in California and Texas. His research found that (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11127-016-0340-9), “propositions are not advantaged by being listed at the top compared to the bottom of the ballot.”
Other scholars, however, have shown (https://academic.oup.com/restud/article-abstract/83/2/460/2461249) that there is something to the concept of “choice fatigue,” or voters not voting for all of the measures on the ballot when given a long list of decisions. A 2016 study showed that, without choice fatigue, “abstentions would decrease by 8 percent, and 6% of the propositions in our data set would have passed rather than failed.”
Meanwhile, voters are not pleased (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) with long ballots. 77 percent of voters in a recent Public Policy Institute of California poll said there were too many propositions on the state ballot.
Which gets us back to the main question – why are politicians playing around with the numbers of ballot measures? It’s not for good government, that’s for sure. That they feel compelled to do so, when the research shows it has a negligible impact on people’s votes despite their displeasure with the significant numbers of ballot measures, says it all.

In summary
Tens of thousands of affordable units across California are stuck in financial purgatory, according to a new report. Will more money get them moving?
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
The apartment building planned on East Morris Avenue in Modesto is exactly the kind of thing that California’s political leaders want to see a whole lot more of: The project promises 44 units of affordable housing — half reserved for people without homes. It’s received zoning approval, weathered public feedback, earned the support of local elected officials and sits beside a busy bus line. Once built, the project promises on-site mental health services, job training and Zumba classes.
What the project lacks is money.
Having quilted together a financial patchwork of local government and corporate grants, private debt, and a plot of land donated by a foundation, it remains just shy of the total needed to break ground.
Six years and 13 funding applications after it was first proposed, the Morris Village project sits ready, but waiting.
An estimated 39,880 affordable units across California are stuck in financial purgatory, according to a new report (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline) by Enterprise Community Partners, a national nonprofit that funds, consults and advocates for affordable housing. That’s 461 “shovel-ready developments” that, like the one on East Morris, are fully designed, legally green-lit and backed with a significant — but still insufficient — amount of money.
Many have “been sitting for a year or two waiting for funding,” said Justine Marcus, policy director for Enterprise’s Northern California office and one of the report’s co-authors. “There’s no exit route right now. It’s a bottleneck.”
For many developers and affordable housing advocates, that bottleneck represents an especially frustrating inconsistency of California public policy. Lawmakers are desperate to see the state build more homes — of all kinds, but especially for people with the least ability to pay the state’s exorbitant rents. State housing regulators have ordered local governments to plan for the construction of an additional 2.5 million units (https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/94729ab1648d43b1811c1698a748c136) by the end of the decade. One million of those are supposed to be for people making less than 80% of each region’s median income.
As a general rule, that’s a population of hard-up renters that the private market has been unable to profitably serve at scale. To fill that gap, non-profit low-income housing developers typically turn to taxpayer-funded support. At the moment, according to the report, there isn’t enough of that to go around.
Enterprise took publicly available but hard-to-parse applicant lists from seven subsidy programs administered by various wings of California’s state government going back three years. With a combination of number crunching and a little inference, the report estimates that clearing the current backlog would require an extra $4.1 billion, split between state administered grants, low-cost loans and tax write-offs.
Once awarded, this final layer of state subsidy has to be spent in relatively short order. That means this list of 39,880 units comprise a group of affordable housing projects that are all but ready to go, said Marcus. “They kinda have to have their (stuff) together.”
Case in point: Two-thirds of the projects on the list have already received support from at least one other state program. Those dollars aren’t awarded to just any developer, said Betsy McGovern-Garcia, vice president of Self-Help Enterprises, one of two non-profits behind Morris Village.
“These are all projects that are close to amenities,” she said. “These are all projects providing resident services. These are all projects that are financially feasible…They are all meeting the bar for what we want to see as a state out of our affordable housing community.”
